text:
Unofficial
English Translation

Firebombing
of the library of a Jewish school–Terrorist and racist acts–Eight (8) months
in preventive detention – Sentence two (2) years as of this date.

COURT OF QUEBEC

CANADA

PROVINCE
OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

"Criminal
and Penal Division"

No:

500-01-006651-043

DATE:

January 18, 2005

___________________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:
THE HONOURABLE JEAN SIROIS, J.C.Q.

___________________________________________________________________________

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN,

Complainant

v.

SLEIMAN EL-MERHEBI

Accused

___________________________________________________________________________

SENTENCE

____________________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

On December 16, 2004, Sleiman El-Merhebi, 19 years old, pleaded
guilty to one count of arson pursuant to
section 434
of the
Criminal Code
,
for having set fire to the library of a Jewish elementary school.

THE FACTS

[
2
]

In the weeks leading up to the commission of this crime, a
Palestinian leader, Sheik Ahmed Yasine, met a violent end. Television news
carried the story. The accused, a Muslim born in Lebanon who has resided in Quebec since the age of seven, was devastated by this event. He blamed Israel for Yasine’s death.

Two days before the firebombing, the
accused bought six (6) drums of kerosene at a Canadian Tire store, where he
worked part-time, and fashioned an incendiary bomb.

[
3
]

On April 5, 2004 at
2:33 a.m., he smashed the window of the library, tossed in his "Molotov Cocktail” and left a tract at the scene
explaining his actions. The text read as follows:

[
translation
]

This is where your crimes and your occupation lead to.
This is in response to your assassinations. This is where the terrorist Ariel
Sharon
is leading you.

Today our target was an empty place. Our goal was only
to send a wake-up call without causing casualties, but this is only the
beginning. If your crimes in the
Middle East
continue, so will our attacks.

We aren’t targeting
Quebec
; you – Israelis and Zionists – you are our target.
The next time, we will hit harder.

Be ready.

The Sheik Ahmed Yasine Brigade

[
4
]

Immediately after his actions, the accused returned to a party, as
he had already laid the groundwork for his alibi. But he left behind numerous
clues that facilitated the police investigation. For example, the kerosene
drums that had been used were sold exclusively at Canadian Tire and had been
purchased at an outlet where the accused worked, not far from the firebombed
school. Police easily traced sales receipts and a videotape of the purchase and
put the accused under electronic surveillance. They then provoked him by
conducting an investigation at his place of work.

The police were thus able to record a
conversation between the accused and a friend in which the accused tells his
friend about his crime, says that he is afraid of being caught as a result of
some mistakes he made, wonders how he could escape his predicament and
contemplates leaving the country.

[
5
] On May 14, the police arrested the
accused and searched his home. They found sticky tape similar to the type used
to hold the drums together, a pair of charred gloves, handwritten notes about a
trip abroad and a biological substance on the sticky paper holding the tract
together that corresponded to the accused’s DNA. The accused has been held in
custody since this arrest.

[
6
] The fire caused considerable damage to
the library of the United Talmud Torah: reconstruction and related costs have exceeded
$600,000. The students, their parents, employees and directors of the school
and the entire Jewish community in Canada were severely traumatized by the event. The whole country,
including the Muslim community, was shaken. There was a general outpouring of
solidarity, which included visits to the school by the Prime Minister of Canada
and the Premier of Quebec.

THE EVIDENCE

[
7
] The Crown called witnesses to testify
regarding the consequences of the firebombing. The school’s principal, Saly
Benamron, testified that her personal and professional life had been turned
upside down. She worked day and night to try to manage a situation for which
she was not prepared. She had to reassure students and parents, attend numerous
meetings, oversee the rebuilding and institute oppressive security measures,
which are still in place and which are less than desirable in an elementary
school. She still suffers from fatigue and insomnia. Everyone—employees,
teachers, students, their families and friends, the Jewish community in Montreal and the broader Jewish community— has
been affected by this crime, which she labels a hate crime.

[
8
] Janice Gerson, Co-President of the
school’s parents’ committee, mother of two children, one of whom attends the
school, and a lawyer by profession, said the crime was an act of anti-semitism
that profoundly shocked her. She now feels insecure in a country known for its
tolerance and expresses regret for the climate of fear that now permeates the
school.

[
9
] M
tre

Rachel
Cohen, Chair of the school’s Board of Directors, testified regarding the extent
of the damages and the costs of reconstruction, which run somewhere between
$600,000 and $700,000. The Crown also filed victim impact statements from a
school worker and the Quebec Director General of B’nai Brith. Their statements
describe the traumatic fall-out of this fire, both at the school and in the
wider Jewish community. An atmosphere of fear now prevails, and many worry that
other Jewish institutions will be targeted. Some parents have even withdrawn
their children from the Jewish school as a protective measure.

[
10
] In defence, counsel for the accused
first called Louis Morissette, a psychiatrist from the Institut Pinel, to
assess the dangerousness of the accused and to determine his state of mind
during the attack. The accused is from a functional family and is the eldest of
four children, three of whom are girls. Like other members of the family, he is
not particularly religious. He is well integrated into Quebec society and completed his Secondary V studies without any
particular difficulty, aside from some discipline problems. He does not follow
international events. Aside from his impulsiveness and immaturity, his past was
not a predictor of his actions. At school, he was often involved in fights due to
his desire to control situations. He acted out of a wish to defend a cause, but
now realizes he was misguided. He does not understand how he could have done
what he did, and expresses profound regret for his actions. He accepts the
consequences of his deed. Given his past and his reflection while in custody,
Dr. Morissette has determined that the dangerousness of the accused is minimal.

[
11
] The accused’s father, Khaleb
El-Merhebi, explained that he came to Quebec alone in 1988, fleeing civil war in Lebanon. His family followed four years later. He came to Canada in search of peace and security and
was surprised by his son’s actions. The family is close-knit, and his son is a
good boy who does not pose any problems. He apologized to the Jewish community and
to Quebec generally for what
happened.

[
12
] The accused’s brother and several
family friends testified on behalf of the accused. Others sent letters. All
were surprised by his crime, saying it did not at all reflect his personality.
They pleaded for the Court’s clemency. It should be noted, however, that school
records document the accused’s impulsiveness and his need to win respect, which
led him into conflict with adults at his school. At one point, he was obliged
to write a letter to his teacher apologizing for his rudeness.

[
13
] The accused testified in court. He
filed his
curriculum vitae
and a written apology drafted two weeks
earlier at the request of his lawyer. This letter contains the conclusions of
his reflection during his seven months in preventive detention. He apologizes
and asks the Jewish community and the students of the school in particular to
forgive him. He also seeks forgiveness from his community and from people of
all races and religions. He admits there was no justification for his actions,
which run counter to his own values and to the values of society. He admits he
should have found some other way to express his disagreement with events in the
Middle East. He writes that he did not intend to incite fear or cause damage,
either psychological or material. While in detention, he took math courses, and
upon his release he would like to return to his family, go to college and live
a balanced life.

He finds it difficult to explain what led
him to set the fire in the library of the Jewish school. He mentions weakness,
irresponsibility and immaturity. He was deeply affected by the violence shown
on television coverage of events in the Middle East. He did not really mean or plan to do everything he wrote in his tract;
rather, it was a way to express his emotions. The Sheik Ahmed Yasine Brigade
does not really exist; it was just a form of signature.

POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

[
14
] Speaking for the Crown, Mtre Anne
Aubé stressed the heinous nature of this crime, which she characterized as a
terrorist act. She has no evidence that any terrorist group was involved, but
she doubts the accused acted alone. She highlighted several aggravating facts:
premeditation, fabrication of an alibi, using an incendiary bomb, targeting an
elementary school, the monetary amount of the damage. It was an attack on one
of the fundamental values of this country, namely multiculturalism. A foreign
conflict served as the premise for targeting a particular community, for
intimidating it, for seeking revenge. M
tre
Aubé cast doubt
on the sincerity of the accused’s remorse, and pointed out that, given the
strong evidence against him, he had no choice but to plead guilty. She has requested
a denunciatory sentence: taking into account the seven months of preventive detention,
which must be counted as double, she seeks a minimum sentence of two years in
prison.

[
15
] On behalf of the accused, Mtre Pierre
Poupart admits that the accused’s actions were inexcusable and that the Montreal Jewish community should not have
to pay for a conflict occurring elsewhere. The accused has been reflecting on
his actions for some time and his letter of apology was not recent, despite the
fact it dates from only 2 weeks ago. Mtre Poupart acknowledges the serious
consequence of this crime on the country’s social peace, but exacting revenge
on the accused will do nothing to improve the situation. He appeals to the
Court’s sense of humanity, forgiveness and compassion. He proposes a sentence
of two years less a day, to be served in the community along with community
service.

ANALYSIS OF THE EVIDENCE

[
16
] First, the accused’s crime must be characterized
using the correct terminology. D
r
Morissette used the term "vandalism” when in fact all the evidence points towards an act of terrorism. The
accused himself acknowledged this when he said to a friend in a taped
conversation (RS-3 p.6): [
translation
:]
"
This isn’t vandalism, it’s

terrorism
". The tract left
at the crime scene leaves no doubt: the accused meant to sow fear by
threatening a harder strike the next time. There is a distinction to be made
between vandalism and terrorism: the former is mindless destruction, while the
latter aims to intimidate, to spread fear for political ends. Terrorism is much
more threatening for society; it attacks its very foundation. This is why the
Courts have always been more severe in punishing terrorism, especially when it
is linked to foreign conflicts that do not involve Canada. Parliament has recognized this in
section 718.2
(
a
)(
v
)
of the
Criminal Code
by including it in the aggravating circumstances that
the Court must consider before sentencing.

[
17
] This same section adds as an
aggravating circumstance the fact that the crime is motivated by prejudice or
hate based on national or ethnic origin or on religion. This is the case here.
The tract leaves no doubt as to the accused’s feelings. The fire targeted
Israelis and Zionists and was directly aimed at Montreal’s Jewish community. He holds them responsible for the State of
Israel’s acts in Palestine and
threatens to continue the attacks if the situation doesn’t change.

AGGRAVATING FACTORS

[
18
]    ●
Seriousness of the offence
: the
maximum sentence provided by Parliament is 14 years in prison. This was a
terrorist act motivated by revenge, hate and prejudice toward a cultural
community, which are aggravating factors specifically mentioned in the
Criminal
Code
.

•

Elementary school firebombed
: the accused targeted the library of an elementary school, an
institution close to the heart of a cultural community, causing damages
exceeding $600,000. Over and above the act’s symbolism, children were targeted
and affected by this violent act; their innocence was attacked.

•

Premeditation
:
this act of vengeance was planned, albeit not for long. The accused chose his
target, bought kerosene two days in advance, and carefully constructed an alibi
that he planned to use. He knew very well what he was doing. The conversation
taped a month later shows that what he regretted was not his crime, but the
mistakes he made that could get him arrested. He showed no empathy toward his
victims, although he was conscious of the seriousness of what he did—an act of
terrorism. His sole concern was escaping; he thought of leaving the country.

•

Tract
: the tract
the accused left on the scene reveals his intent, which was to exact revenge on
Montreal’s Jewish community for
acts committed elsewhere and to spread fear by threatening to strike harder
next time. This tract had the effect of further intimidating the Jewish
community.

•

Consequences
:
several witnesses testified to the serious impact of this act of terrorism on
the Jewish community in general and on the school’s employees, teachers,
students and parents in particular. The trauma is aggravated by the fact that
the Jewish community has often been the victim of racism and hatred. The
school’s principal was obliged to implement security measures not normally
found in an elementary school.

MITIGATING FACTORS

[
19
]
●

The accused’s
age
: he was 18½ at the time of the offence, and 19 now.

•

No criminal record
: either as a juvenile or an adult.

•

The guilty plea
:
the accused entered a guilty plea prior to the calling of witnesses before the
preliminary inquiry. However, he did not do so at the earliest opportunity; he
waited seven months. In addition, the weight of the evidence against him left
him with little choice.

•

Remorse
: the
accused has filed a letter in which he apologizes to everyone affected by his
act and shows evidence of remorse. It is not clear whether his regret is
sincere or disingenuous, but we must give him the benefit of the doubt in that
regard. In any event, what is important is that he expressed regret,
acknowledged that he was irresponsible and demonstrated his desire to change
his ways, thereby defusing the threats in his tract. Despite his reflections, however,
he was not really able to explain to the Court the motivation for his act.

•

Isolated act
: in
the opinion of the parties and witnesses, this was an isolated act, totally
inconsistent with his past. The Crown has no evidence of any connection with a
racist or terrorist organization, and the amateurish nature of the crime–the
accused inadvertently left many clues for detection–seems to refute any such
theory. The accused attended a multiethnic school and, despite some
disciplinary problems, did not demonstrate any racism. He was going out with a
girl of South-American background and of a different religion.

•

Healthy environment
: the accused comes from a functional family that disapproves of
such acts and can provide him with a structured environment when he comes out
of prison. He can also count on the support of many friends.

•

Dangerousness
:
According to Dr. Morissette, the accused poses little danger and his past is a
good indicator of the future. Dr. Morissette is probably right: during his
period of reflection the accused has become more mature and thoughtful. We
cannot be sure, however. Indeed, nothing in the accused’s past indicated that he
would commit this crime, but he did, in fact, plan and commit it anyway. The
accused did not follow current events and was not religious, yet he reacted
strongly to an event that took place thousands of kilometres from his home.
Even he cannot explain why he did what he did, other than that he acted out of
emotion, impulsively and irresponsibly. It is to be hoped that detention will
dissolve all the risk factors that were present before his arrest. Indeed, the
Court had a legitimate reason to deny his release pending trial, as his tract
indicated he was prepared to go further. Would he have in fact committed other
crimes? No one can be certain.

PURPOSE AND PRINCIPLES OF SENTENCING

[
20
] In the
Criminal Code
,
Parliament has set forth the purpose and principles the Court must consider in
sentencing:

718.
Purpose –
The fundamental purpose of sentencing is to
contribute, along with crime prevention initiatives, to respect for the law and
the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society by imposing just sanctions
that have one or more of the following objectives:

a)

to denounce unlawful
conduct ;

b)

to deter the offender
and other persons from committing offences;

c)

to separate offenders
from society, where necessary
;

d)

to assist in
rehabilitating offenders ;

e)

to provide reparations
for harm done to victims or to the community;

f)

to promote a sense of
responsibility in offenders, and acknowledgment of the harm done to victims and
to the community."

718.1
Fundamental Principle-
A sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the
offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender."

718.2
Other Sentencing Principles-
A court that imposes a sentence shall also
take into consideration the following principles :

a)

a sentence should be
increased or reduced to account for any relevant aggravating or mitigating
circumstances relating to the offence or the offender; shall be deemed to be
aggravating circumstances:

(i)

evidence that the
offence was motivated by prejudice or hate based on race, national or ethnic
origin, language, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or physical disability or
sexual orientation,

(ii)

evidence that the
offender, in committing the offence, abused the offender’s spouse or common-law
partner or child,

(iii)

evidence that the
offender, in committing the offence, abused a position of trust or authority in
relation to the victim,

(iv)

evidence that the
offence was committed for the benefit of, at the direction of or in association
with a criminal organization, or,

(v)

evidence that the
offence was a terrorism offence;

b)

a sentence should be
similar to sentences imposed on similar offenders for similar offences
committed in similar circumstances;

c)

where consecutive
sentences are imposed, the combined sentence should not be unduly long or
harsh;

d)

an offender should not
be deprived of liberty if less restrictive sanctions may be appropriate in the
circumstances and;

e)

all available sanctions
other than imprisonment that are reasonable in the circumstances should be
considered for all offenders, with particular attention to the circumstances of
aboriginal offenders.

[
21
] Denouncing the crime committed by the
accused is no doubt the most important criteria in this case. The Court must,
without equivocation, denounce any act of terrorism, whatever its motivation,
in order to maintain social peace, especially in light of the current context
of the global spreading of terrorism. Quebec has experienced politically motivated terrorism in the past, and
the Courts’ response was categorical. Today, the situation has changed, and
ideological, cultural and religious differences as well as international
conflicts have become motivating factors behind acts of hatred, vandalism and
terrorism.

We cannot tolerate individuals or groups
attacking citizens of this country, whatever their origin, religion or
ideology, in order to promote their cause. We cannot tolerate acts of racism,
hate or intolerance in a country that guarantees freedom of conscience,
religion, thought, belief, opinion and expression (section 2 of the
Charter
),
a country that values its multicultural heritage (section 27 of the
Charter
).
Canadian courts have expounded on these principles on many occasions and have
vigorously denounced all manifestations of terrorism.

In
R.
v.
Sandouga
,
2002 ABCA 196 (CanLII)
, 2002
A.B.C.A. 196, Justice Fruman of the Alberta Court of Appeal offered the
following comments on terrorism:

At para. [26]:
Terrorist acts take on special public
dimension because of the importance Canadians place on multiculturalism. We
welcome immigrants from diverse nations, and encourage them to retain their
heritage and distinct cultural identities, a policy enshrined in s. 27 of the
Charter. With this privilege comes the corresponding obligation to respect the
dignity and cultural identity of others.
Canada

does not punish people for their political beliefs or social values, as long as
they are expressed in lawful ways. But our tolerance ends when political
ideology manifests itself in terrorist acts, involving violence to others or
destruction of their property
.

Para. [27]:
Unfortunately, acts of terrorism have broad
repercussions. They are rarely isolated incidents, but “invite imitation and repetition
by others, and incite retaliation
: R. v. Ingram and Grimsdale
(1977),
1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA)
,
35
C.C.C. (2d) 376
at 379 (Ont.
C.A.
)
.

Such
actions therefore threaten the fabric of
Canada
’s
multicultural, pluralistic society
.
See
R. v. Soles,
[1998] O.J. No. 5061, (O.J.)
at para. 20 (Gen. Div.)
;
R. v. Lelas
(
1990),
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
,
58 C.C.C. (3d) 568
at 574-75 (Ont.
C.A.
)
;

Ingram and Grimsdale
, supra
,
at 379
.
Because these repugnant activities must be
discouraged, the primary objectives in imposing a sentence for a terrorist act
are denunciation and general deterrence.

The British Columbia Court of Appeal also
denounced terrorism inspired by foreign conflicts by citing the comments of the
trial judge:

…
Acts of violence are not to be perpetrated
on Canadian soil in order to advance some foreign cause. Failure to mete out a
lengthy penal sentence would be inimical to the public good and would tend to
lessen society’s confidence in the legal system
…

R
. v.
Atwal et al.
(1990)
1990 CanLII 10930 (BC CA)
, 57
C.C.C. (3d) 143, p.145 (BCCA).

This Court must also denounce this expression
of racism and intolerance toward a community that has frequently been the
target of attacks. Canadian courts have always unanimously denounced racist
acts directed at cultural communities. For example, we cite the Ontario Court
of Appeal in
R.
v.
Lelas
,
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
, 58 C.C.C. (3d) 568, p. 569

…
An offence which is directed against a
particular racial or religious group is more heinous, as it attacks the very
fabric of society
.…

…
The accused’s acts were done to strike fear
and terror and to cause emotional upset in the Jewish community. When mischief
is racially or religiously motivated and is done to cause emotional injury or
shock to a particular segment of Canadian society it calls for a far more
severe penalty than mischief which is done merely to damage property
.…

[
22
] General and individual deterrence is
another factor taken into consideration by the courts in these kinds of
situations. Even if the accused seems to have understood, the Court must send a
clear message to all who might be tempted to imitate his acts that they will be
dealt with harshly. The Court is aware that no sentence can deter a
professional terrorist, but it hopes that the sentence imposed will force those
who, like the accused, act on impulse to stop and reflect. Placing the accused
in preventive detention is not sufficient  to meet this criterion of general
deterrence.

In
Sandouga
, cited above, Justice
Fruman expressed the following opinion on the necessity of a deterrent sentence
in circumstances similar to those in this case:

Par. [28]:
This sentencing principle appears
consistently in cases involving violent acts of terrorism. The sentence “must
be one which expresses the public abhorrence for such conduct and their refusal
to countenance it”:
Ingram and Grimsdale
, supra, at 379. When an offence
“involves a violent act of international terrorism performed in a country
unconnected with the place in which the alleged injustices have been
perpetrated, the need for an unusually strong general deterrent prevails”:
R.
v. Balian

(1988),
29 O.A.C. 387
at 389 (
C.A.
)
.
In sentencing for acts of terrorism, “deterrence must be considered to be of
paramount importance. The sentence imposed must be sufficient to bring home to
others contemplating a similar terrorist act that this type of conduct will not
be tolerated, nor will it be treated lightly by the courts”:
R. v. Atwal

(1990),
1990 CanLII 10930 (BC CA)
,
57 C.C.C. (3d) 143
at 145 (BCCA)
, quoting Callaghan J.’s unreported
trial decision. “Conduct fostered by philosophies and beliefs that condone and
extol violence as a means of disapproval of those perceived to be in opposition
to those philosophies and beliefs must be sternly denounced by the courts”:

R. v. Simms
(1990),
1990 ABCA 352 (CanLII)
,
60 C.C.C. (3d) 499
at 507 (Alta. C.A.)
.

The same principle was approved by the
British Columbia Court of Appeal in
R.
v.
Atwal
, cited above, at 145,
and which reads as follows:

…
The sentence imposed must be sufficient to
bring home to others contemplating a similar terrorist act that this type of
conduct will not be tolerated, nor will it be treated lightly by the courts
.…

[
23
] In handing down a just and
appropriate sentence, the Court will consider all mitigating factors, but notes
that the principle of rehabilitation must give way to those of denunciation and
general deterrence. The sentence imposed must be proportional to the gravity of
the offence and the degree of responsibility of the accused. As with all
sentences, it must be the lightest possible in keeping with the philosophy of
the Canadian legal system in sentencing matters, all the while respecting the
objectives set out by Parliament. In order to maintain public confidence in the
courts, it must be in keeping with sentences imposed for similar offences
committed in similar circumstances. In this regard, we refer to decisions cited
by the parties.

THE CASE LAW

[
24
]     ➢
R
. v.
Sandouga

(2002) A.B.C.A. (cited above)

The accused
threw a Molotov Cocktail at a synagogue to show his anger at the Jewish
community for the situation in the Middle East. Damage was minimal and only affected an exterior wall. The accused
suffered burns. He was 20 years old and had no criminal record. The 12-month
sentence was increased to 30 months by the Alberta Court of Appeal on the
grounds the trial judge had not given enough weight to the criteria of
denunciation and general deterrence.

➢

R
. v.
Lelas
,
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
, 58
C.C.C
.
(3d) 568 (cited above)

The accused
scrawled anti-Semitic slogans on a synagogue and a Jewish school. He was 22,
with no criminal record, but was a member of the Ku-Klux-Klan. The sentence was
increased from 6 months to 1 year in prison.

➢

R
. v.
Creagham

Alta. C.A.
(1991) AJ 560

This was a case
of hate graffiti directed at the Jewish community, but written on a church, the
accused having mistaken the building for a synagogue. They were not part of any
organized group. The accused paid $1,000 in damages and were sentenced to 200
hours of community service.

➢

R
. v.
Soles,
(1998)
O.J. No. 5061

This case
involved vandalism in a Jewish cemetery, a crime with racial overtones. A
sentence of 10 months incarceration was added to four months detention pending
trial for the equivalent of 18 months in prison.

➢

R
. v.
Bettger
,
(1995)
N.W.T.J. 88

– Supreme Court of the
North-West
Territories

The accused set off an explosion in a mine during
a labour dispute, causing $115,000 in damages. Sentences of 36 and 30 months
were imposed.

➢

R
. v.
Thurston
,
(1994)
A.J. 364 (Alta.
C.A.
)

The accused, a member of the Animal Liberation Front,
set fire to 3 trucks. The fire spread to a building housing a fish factory,
causing $55,000 in damages. The accused attacked a university lab, causing more
than $66,000 in damages. The trial judge handed down a suspended sentence in
light of the 15 months of  preventive detention. The Court of Appeal increased
the sentence to 2 years less a day, or the equivalent of 54 months in prison.
The accused was in possession of a stash of weapons, ammunition and explosives.
The Court of Appeal criticized the trial judge for not given enough weight to
the seriousness of the offence, general deterrence and protection of the public.

DETERMINATION
OF THE SENTENCE

[
25
] The defence is asking for a sentence
of two years less a day, to be served in the community. The Court cannot accept
this recommendation, because it does not satisfy the criteria relating to the seriousness
of the offence, denunciation and general deterrence, which must take priority
here. On this point, Chief Justice Lamer of the Supreme Court of Canada stated the
following:

R
. v.
Proulx

2000 SCC 5 (CanLII)
, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 61, No. 26376 (at para. 114)

…When
punishment objectives such as denunciation and deterrence are particularly
pressing, for example in the case of aggravating circumstances, incarceration
will generally be the favoured sanction, and this despite the fact that a
conditional sentence could also [page 121] meet rehabilitation objectives…

Mtre Poupart appeals to the Court’s sense
of humanity, compassion and forgiveness in order to promote these values and
nurture understanding and tolerance. It is a wise message and one put into
practice continually by the courts, which repeatedly hold that sentences must
not be imposed out of vengeance to quiet public outcry. On the other hand, to
give too much weight to these principles risks backfiring and runs against the
grain of sentencing principles set down by Parliament in the
Criminal Code
.

[
26
] The Crown proposes a minimum sentence
of two years in prison, leaving the exact duration to the Court’s discretion.
The Court considers that the sentence should not be less than two years,
because anything less would not meet the sentencing principles mentioned above.
A sentence of 2 years as of this date is equivalent to a sentence of 40 months
because detention pending trial has lasted 8 months. According to the case law,
such detention must count as double, because during detention the accused was
deprived of privileges, in particular parole.

In my view, this sentence is adequate
because it is in keeping with the criteria of seriousness, denunciation and
general deterrence, while at the same time it takes into account the victim’s
character and avoids making him a scapegoat for terrorism generally.

A sentence must be the most lenient
possible while at the same time respecting the elements taken into
consideration by the Court. A harsher sentence is in my view unnecessary,
especially given that the Crown itself considers that two years is the minimum
sentence to be handed down in this case.

[
27
]
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT
IMPOSES THE FOLLOWING SENTENCE:

SENTENCES
the
accused to 40 months in prison, from which must be subtracted the period of preventive
detention, equalling 16 months. The sentence is therefore two years of
prison from the date of this judgement.

FORBIDS
the
accused to have in his possession any firearm, cross-bow, prohibited weapon,
restricted weapon, prohibited device, ammunition, prohibited ammunition and
explosive substance, for a period of 10 years, pursuant to
section 109
of the
Criminal
Code
;

EXEMPTS
the
accused from a victim-fine surcharge.
